summary: Specifies Atom, an XML-based format for syndicating web content and metadata, such as news feeds and blog posts. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Atom is a standard XML format for a feed of related entries, such as posts or headlines. Each entry has required information so different feed readers can identify and process it.

questions: what is the atom syndication format
what is atom id used for
what fields are required in an atom entry
subtitle: An XML format for publishing feeds of entries and their metadata.

tldr.problem: Web publishers need a structured format for sharing lists of related items with websites and software that read feeds.
tldr.mechanism: Atom defines XML feed and entry documents with standard fields for identifiers, titles, update times, people, links and content.
tldr.outcome: Atom documents use the application/atom+xml media type and allow extensions, signatures and encryption. RFC 4287 is updated by RFC 5988.

today: RFC 4287 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2005. It has been updated by RFC 5988.

sections.title: Feeds, Entries and Atom Documents
sections.content:
An Atom feed is a list of related information, made up of entries with attached metadata. The main use is syndicating web content such as weblog posts and news headlines. The format uses the namespace http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom.

The RFC defines Atom Feed Documents, whose root element is atom:feed, and Atom Entry Documents, whose root is atom:entry. Both are XML 1.0 documents identified with application/atom+xml. They must be well-formed XML, but the RFC does not require a document type definition.
sections.plainLanguage: A feed groups entries, and each entry describes one item. Atom provides fixed XML document forms for a whole feed or one entry.

sections.title: Shared Forms for Text, People and Dates
sections.content:
Atom reuses three constructs. A Text construct contains human-readable text with a type of text, html or xhtml; plain text is the default. A Person construct must contain exactly one atom:name and may contain one URI and one e-mail address.

Date constructs follow RFC 3339's date-time format. They use an uppercase T between date and time, and an uppercase Z when no numeric time-zone offset is present. Atom documents may also use xml:base for relative references and xml:lang for natural language.
sections.plainLanguage: Atom uses shared rules for readable text, people and dates. These rules help software interpret the same fields consistently.

sections.title: Required Feed and Entry Fields
sections.content:
A feed MUST contain exactly one atom:id, atom:title and atom:updated. It must contain an author unless each entry has one. A feed SHOULD include a link with rel="self" that gives the preferred URI for retrieving it.

An entry MUST contain exactly one ID, title and updated time. An entry without content needs an alternate link. It also needs a summary when content is linked externally or encoded as Base64. The content element can contain text or point to content elsewhere using src.
sections.plainLanguage: A feed and each entry have an identifier, a title and an update time. An entry also provides its content or a link to an alternate version.

sections.title: Identifiers, Links and Metadata
sections.content:
An atom:id is a permanent, universally unique IRI. It must not change when a document is moved, copied or republished. Processors compare IDs character by character, case-sensitively, and must not assume that an ID can be retrieved by dereferencing it.

Links use an href IRI and an optional relation. If rel is absent, it means alternate. Other metadata elements describe authors, categories, generators, icons, logos, publication time, rights and source feeds. An updated time records a significant change as judged by the publisher.
sections.plainLanguage: An entry's ID stays the same when the entry moves or is copied. Links and other metadata describe related pages, authors, categories and dates.

sections.title: Signing and Encrypting Documents
sections.content:
An Atom feed or entry may carry an XML digital signature. A processor must continue processing a signed document even when it cannot verify the signature. A processor that does verify signatures must support exclusive XML canonicalization and RSA signature verification; DSA verification is not required.

The root element may be encrypted. A processor that decrypts Atom documents must support AES-128 in CBC mode. Because encryption alone does not guarantee integrity, the RFC recommends checking a signature or another document hash. If a document is both signed and encrypted, sign it first and then encrypt it.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature can identify the signer and detect changes, while encryption hides the content. Encryption alone does not show that the content stayed unchanged.

sections.title: Extensions and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Atom allows markup from other XML vocabularies in permitted locations. A processor that does not understand such markup must not stop processing or report an error. Some unknown elements can be skipped; in text and content constructs, processors should ignore the markup while retaining its text.

Atom content may contain HTML or XHTML, including elements that can expose a processor to executable content. The RFC calls for care when handling such content. It also warns that an attacker can reuse another publisher's entry ID, so processors may need to check the source before treating matching IDs as duplicates.
sections.plainLanguage: Extensions let publishers add information, and readers should keep working when they meet an extension they do not know. Readers also need to handle embedded web markup and IDs with care.
